chapter: The Strange Knight and Squire, Challenge, Victory and Transformation (the middle of it)

facts: The strange knight finished his sentence from the page before: the tasks Casildea set him were like those imposed on Hercules by his stepmother
One time she ordered him to challenge the famous giant-woman of Seville, commonly called La Giralda
He described La Giralda as stout and strong as brass, and as the most changeable and fickle woman in the world, though she never moves from where she is
He boasted that he came, saw and conquered, and made her stay still for a week even though the wind blew constantly
He was next commanded to weigh the great antique bulls of Guisando, a task he said was more fitting to porters than to a knight-errant
Another time she required him to plunge into the abyss of Cabra and tell her what was down there
He said he has done all these things and still his hopes are unfulfilled
He said her disdain continues and her tyrannical commands go on
Her newest order is that he cross all the provinces of Spain and force every knight-errant he meets to confess something

glossary.Hercules: The most popular of the ancient Greek heroes, a son of Zeus and a mortal mother. Zeus' wife Hera hated him and drove him insane, and while mad he killed his wife and children. To atone he performed twelve feats, called his labors, all thought to be impossible, among them killing the nine-headed Hydra and lifting the world off Atlas' shoulders to get the golden apples of Hesperides.
glossary.bulls of Guisando: Ancient carved figures near the city of Avila.
glossary.Cabra: A deep cave in the province of Cordoba.

facts: The thing every knight-errant must confess is that Casildea is the best and most beautiful of women, and that he himself is the bravest and most adoring knight in the world
He claimed to have crossed Spain from end to end and defeated all the knights who dared oppose him
He named one of them especially: Don Quixote de la Mancha, whom he says he compelled to confess that Casildea is more beautiful than Dulcinea
He considered his conquest of Don Quixote equal to the defeat of all the knights of the world, since Don Quixote had defeated them all, so that he reaps all of Don Quixote's glory and fame
Don Quixote answered quietly that he says nothing about the other victories, but does not admit that the stranger has vanquished Don Quixote de la Mancha
He said the stranger may have overcome someone resembling him, but certainly not the man himself
The knight of the wood exclaimed how not the man himself, and swore the contrary
He described the man: tall, with a long lean face and a hooked nose bent to one side, gray-haired, lanky-limbed, with a heavy drooping mustache
He added that the man calls himself the Knight of the Sad Face, or the Sorrowful Countenance
He added that the man has for his squire a peasant by the name of Sancho, for his horse a steed named Rocinante, and for his lady-love Dulcinea del Toboso

glossary.I came, I saw, I conquered: A famous quote from the Roman emperor Julius Caesar, who said it to explain the ease of one of his victories in battle. In Latin the phrase is Veni, vidi, vici.

facts: The stranger finished his description: the lady-love is sometimes called Aldonza Lorenzo
He said that if that is not enough to prove he is telling the truth, here is his sword, which will force belief on the most incredulous
Don Quixote answered softly, asking to be listened to for a moment
He said the man the stranger speaks of is a particular friend of his, and that though the description is fairly accurate on the whole, he is certain it is not the man in question
He said that man has many enemies among the enchanters, one in particular
He suggested one of these enchanters may have impersonated him and allowed himself to be defeated, in order to damage Don Quixote's reputation
He offered as proof that in the last couple of days evil enchanters have transformed the lovely Dulcinea del Toboso into a lowly peasant girl
He said that if the stranger is still dissatisfied, here stands Don Quixote himself in person, ready to prove his identity with his weapons in whatever fashion the stranger prefers
Saying this, Don Quixote stood up, clutched the hilt of his sword, and waited for the knight to make his decision
The strange knight replied quietly that it is not becoming for knight-errants to perform feats of arms in the dark, like highwaymen
He proposed that they wait for daylight
He proposed that the conditions of battle be that the defeated shall obey the command of the victor, so long as the command is something a knight can obey without dishonoring himself
Don Quixote agreed to these conditions, and the two knights went to rouse their squires and order them to prepare for the looming combat
The stranger's squire took the matter coolly enough
Sancho was terribly frightened for his master, and even more for himself
The reason was that the other squire informed him that in this part of Spain it is customary for the squires of combating knights to fight each other also
Sancho said he has never heard of that custom before and is not going by it
He added that he has no sword and has never had one in his life
The other squire said they can get over that difficulty, since they have a couple of linen sacks
His plan was to put half a dozen good-sized stones in the sacks, so the two of them could pound each other quite handsomely
Sancho still objected, saying it was unchristian for two friends who had just been eating and drinking together to begin knocking each other about when they had no reason to quarrel
The other squire answered that if that is all, then before they get started he will come up and knock Sancho down with a few blows, which will make him feel mad enough
Sancho answered that if he tries that, he knows how to stop him with his cudgel
Sancho said he is a man of peace, but a cornered one
